answers.question: Is Luma.Green an 'e-commerce operator' under CGST s.52 (0.5% TCS) and under the Income-tax Act 2025 (the successor to s.194-O, 0.1% TDS) for bookings and trades where money never passes through it? What changes once escrow through a payment aggregator starts?
answers.answer: GST: not during the pilot. CGST s.52(1) only makes an operator collect TCS on supplies "where the consideration with respect to such supplies is to be collected by the operator"; CBIC Circular 194/06/2023-GST (17 July 2023) confirms the collector is the operator that actually releases payment to the supplier, and "net value" counts only supplies by registered persons, so a platform that merely records cash/UPI paid hand-to-hand has no TCS, no s.24(x) registration and no GSTR-8 duty (the rate, if it ever applied, is 0.5% total, 0.25% CGST + 0.25% SGST, since Notification 15/2024-Central Tax of 10 July 2024). Income-tax: very likely yes from day one. The Income-tax Act 2025 (assent 21 Aug 2025, in force 1 April 2026) re-enacts s.194-O as s.393(1) Table Sl. No. 8(v): "any e-commerce operator" deducts 0.1% of the gross amount of sales of goods or services by an "e-commerce participant" that it facilitates, nil threshold, and Note 3(ii) deems any payment made by the purchaser directly to the participant to be paid by the operator, so cash or UPI moving outside the app does not take you out; the s.402(13)-(14) definitions are wide ("owns, operates or manages digital or electronic facility or platform for electronic commerce"; a participant is any resident selling goods through it), and the only published safe harbour, CBDT Circular 20/2021 (25 Nov 2021), covers e-auction portals that do price discovery only with contract, delivery and payment all outside the portal and no knowledge of payment quantum or schedule, conditions Luma.Green's bookings, Saathi pickups, verified counterparties and recorded prices fail. Relief for households: s.393(4) Table Sl. No. 11 exempts an individual/HUF seller whose gross sales through the operator are at most Rs 5 lakh in the tax year and who has furnished PAN or Aadhaar, which covers practically every household, but only if the app captures PAN or Aadhaar, because s.397(2)(b) sets the no-PAN rate for this entry at 5% instead of 0.1%. For the business legs (kabadiwala to yard to recycler to manufacturer) Luma.Green must deduct 0.1% of the gross trade value (GST excluded if shown separately, per CBDT Circular 20/2023 of 28 Dec 2023) at credit or payment, whichever is earlier, deposit it and file TDS returns under its TAN; because it holds no money it must recover that 0.1% from the seller by contract (a monthly debit or offset) or fund it itself, and once it deducts, no other TDS (such as the buyer's 0.1% on purchases over Rs 50 lakh) applies to the same trade. When escrow through a payment aggregator starts, GST flips: Luma.Green then collects the consideration (the PA is only a conduit; under the 2023 circular the operator that releases payment is the collector), so it must register as a TCS collector under s.24(x) in Karnataka and any state where its sellers sit, collect 0.5% on the net value of taxable supplies by registered sellers each month, deposit by the 10th and file GSTR-8 (s.52(3)-(4)); unregistered kabadiwalas selling through a TCS-collecting operator must then register or use the Notification 34/2023-Central Tax route (31 July 2023, in force 1 Oct 2023: PAN, intra-state only, one state, and an enrolment number on the GST portal before any supply, which the platform must gate), the goods threshold being Rs 40 lakh (Karnataka is not a special-category state). Income-tax does not change with escrow except that deduction becomes mechanical: CBDT Circular 17/2020 (29 Sept 2020) says the payment gateway/PA need not deduct where the operator already has. RBI: Luma.Green must not itself pool buyer money and settle sellers; under the RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions 2025 (15 Sept 2025) that is PA business needing authorisation (Rs 15 crore net worth at application, Rs 25 crore by year 3), so use a licensed PA's escrow and expect the PA to KYC every kabadiwala and yard as a merchant, because a PA must ensure a marketplace does not accept payments for sellers not onboarded on its platform. Separately from operator status, since 10 Oct 2024 registered buyers pay GST under reverse charge on metal scrap (tariff chapters 72-81) bought from unregistered sellers and deduct 2% GST TDS on B2B metal-scrap contracts of Rs 2.5 lakh or more; those duties sit on yards and recyclers, not on Luma.Green, but its trade records should carry them.
answers.decision: Treat Luma.Green as an e-commerce operator for income-tax s.393 from 13 Oct 2026 (obtain a TAN now, capture PAN or Aadhaar from every household at sign-up so the Rs 5 lakh exemption applies, deduct 0.1% on all business-to-business trades and recover it from the seller under the platform terms), and treat it as NOT a GST s.52 collector until escrow goes live; the month escrow starts, register under s.24(x), collect 0.5% and file GSTR-8, gate unregistered sellers behind a Notification 34/2023 enrolment number, and route all money through a licensed payment aggregator rather than Luma.Green's own account.
answers.whoToAsk: A chartered accountant who handles TDS/GST for marketplaces, to confirm (a) that recording a booked trade with an offline cash/UPI payment counts as 'facilitating' a sale under s.393 (no CBDT ruling covers a record-only platform), (b) when 'credit' occurs for a trade Luma.Green never pays, and (c) the Karnataka TCS registration set-up before escrow; consider a CBDT advance ruling only if trade volumes justify the cost.

answers.question: Are households 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act when they sell scrap and get a free pickup, and do the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 as amended in 2026 apply to Luma.Green (grievance officer, 48-hour acknowledgement, seller disclosures)? Or should it adopt those norms voluntarily?
answers.answer: For the scrap sale itself, no: s.2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act 2019 makes someone a "consumer" only when they buy goods or hire/avail a service "for a consideration", so a household selling scrap is the seller, and the kabadiwala who buys is expressly excluded as "a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose" (though Explanation (a) keeps a buyer who purchases solely to earn a livelihood by self-employment inside the definition, which many small kabadiwalas would fit). For the free pickup, s.2(42) says "service" "does not include the rendering of any service free of charge", which on its face keeps households out; but in Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (AIR 1996 SC 550) the Supreme Court held that a nominally free service remains a "service" where its cost is borne by paying users or a third party, and here the pickup is paid for out of the kabadiwala's margin and the scrap changing hands, so a Bengaluru district commission could plausibly treat a household as a consumer of the pickup, and the moment Luma.Green charges households anything (priority slot, bins, subscription) they are consumers outright. That point is genuinely unsettled and cannot be closed from public pages. The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 (notified 23 July 2020) apply to "all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic network" and all e-commerce models, and define an "e-commerce entity" as anyone who "owns, operates or manages digital or electronic facility or platform for electronic commerce", so Luma.Green fits on its face; Rule 2's only carve-out is for "any activity of a natural person carried out in a personal capacity", which frees the household seller from seller duties but not the platform. Practitioner analysis (Trilegal, 5 Aug 2020) reads the Rules as governing consumer purchases, so the pure B2B legs (kabadiwala to yard to recycler to manufacturer) fall outside them except where a buyer buys for self-employment livelihood, but the Rules also impose duties toward "users" (anyone who accesses the platform), which is why the same analysis flags ambiguity for B2B platforms. The Amendment Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 789(E), 9 Sept 2026, in force 1 Jan 2027) do not narrow scope or add a small-platform threshold; they keep the 48-hour acknowledgement and one-month resolution (already in the 2020 Rules, as the Ministry's Lok Sabha answer of 25 Mar 2026 records) and add giving the complainant a copy of the complaint, mandatory National Consumer Helpline convergence, display of legal name/HQ address/website/grievance contact, plain-language ranking disclosure, labelled sponsored listings, a 30-day prior-price rule for discounts, an annual dark-pattern self-audit with a displayed certificate, seller GSTIN/MSME identifiers, and express consent before consumer data is used for the platform's own products. One structural trap: Rule 4(1) expects an e-commerce entity to be a company incorporated in India (or a foreign company or office owned by a resident) with a resident nodal person, and the 2020 analysis notes it is unclear whether an LLP qualifies, so check the pilot entity's form. Recommendation: adopt the norms voluntarily from 13 Oct 2026 rather than argue about scope; the cost is one named grievance officer, a published address and contact, a 48-hour/30-day complaint clock, seller (kabadiwala/yard) disclosures you already gather during verification, a plain sentence on how kabadiwalas are ranked, no dark patterns, explicit consent for data, and joining NCH convergence (1,398 companies had by March 2026), which also pre-empts CCPA attention (Rs 3.00 crore of penalties across 477 class-action notices by 9 Mar 2026). Doing this does not concede that households are consumers; word the terms as "user" grievance rights and keep household-facing statements accurate about weights and rates, which is where any unfair-trade-practice complaint would come from.
answers.decision: Adopt the 2020 Rules and the 2026 amendments voluntarily from the pilot start (named grievance officer, 48-hour acknowledgement with a copy of the complaint, 30-day resolution, published legal name/address/contact, verified-business disclosures, a plain explanation of kabadiwala ranking, no dark patterns, express consent for data, NCH convergence enrolment) without conceding that households are 'consumers', and get a one-page counsel opinion on the free-pickup point and on whether the pilot entity's legal form satisfies Rule 4(1) before 1 Jan 2027.
answers.whoToAsk: A Bengaluru consumer-law counsel for (a) whether the free pickup makes households consumers under s.2(42) read with IMA v Shantha, and (b) whether an LLP or partnership satisfies Rule 4(1)'s company requirement; the Department of Consumer Affairs' National Consumer Helpline convergence desk (contact given in the Lok Sabha answer of 25 Mar 2026) to enrol the platform.
